transcript.text: Hi, our integrated fridge freezer (behind a kitchen door) - the fridge is around 10 degrees but the freezer seems ok. We had a power cut a week ago, not sure if related. Rented flat, can't really take it out.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. A fridge at around 10°C is too warm, even if the freezer still appears OK. With that split between compartments, the common causes are a setting or mode changed by the power cut, food blocking the cold-air vents, or—if those are fine—an airflow/defrost fault inside the appliance. Check the fridge control is set to about 3–5°C and that holiday/eco mode is off, then make sure food is not pressed against any vents on the rear wall. Don’t rely on the fridge for high-risk chilled food at 10°C; keep it to a minimum and follow food-label guidance. If the settings and vents are fine, report it to the landlord/agent rather than trying to pull out an integrated unit, as it may need an engineer.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

Thanks. The dial inside is on 3 of 5 and I've got a thermometer in the fridge reading 10C, freezer is about -16C. No burning smell or tripping, it's just running a lot. I can't see any vents on the fridge back wall though, is that normal?

Yes — that can be normal. Some integrated fridge-freezers have no visible fridge vents, especially non-frost-free designs; on others the air outlet is hidden in a trim or duct rather than the back wall. The more useful clue is the freezer: at about -16°C while the fridge is 10°C and it is running a lot, this could be either ice restricting airflow/defrosting, or a reduced cooling-system performance fault. With it switched off and unplugged, look at the freezer’s rear internal wall only—do not remove panels. A thick, solid frost or ice sheet points to a defrost/airflow problem; a mostly clear wall makes a cooling-system fault more likely, which the landlord should arrange an engineer to assess.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
I looked at the freezer back wall and there's some frost on it, but not loads. Not a thick sheet or anything. What does that suggest?

A light amount of frost is usually normal, so it makes a major ice/defrost blockage less likely. Because both compartments are warmer than ideal (especially the fridge) and it is running a lot, the main possibilities are restricted ventilation around the integrated cabinet or reduced cooling performance from the compressor/sealed cooling system. Check the accessible plinth grille below the unit and any vent above the cabinet are not blocked; do not pull the appliance out or remove panels. If those vents are clear, report it to the landlord/agent for an engineer, as a sealed-system or compressor fault is not an owner repair and the fridge at 10°C is not safe for keeping high-risk chilled food.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
The plinth has a vent grille and I can't see anything blocking it. I'm not sure about a vent above the cabinet. Would you say I should just report it to the letting agent then?

Yes — report it to the letting agent now. The main possibilities are poor ventilation around the integrated cabinet, or reduced cooling performance from the compressor/sealed refrigeration system; the latter is not a DIY repair. Ask them to arrange an appliance engineer and include the measured temperatures and that it followed a power cut. Keep high-risk chilled food out of the fridge until it is maintaining 5°C or below.
